title: Looped core block
question: Does one shared core block looped r times match a deeper unshared model with far fewer parameters? Does quality keep improving when r at test time exceeds r in training?
prediction: Written 2026-11-22 before the run. At r=4 (about 2x E0's FLOPs/token, 11% fewer non-emb params), val loss matches E0 within +-3%, so we expect no win per token yet; the claim to test is the r curve. Predicted shape: r=1 clearly worse (> +10% vs r=4); r=2 < r=1; r=4 about r=6 (flat); r=8 about the same or slightly better than r=4; r=12 (beyond the trained max of 7) flat or slightly worse, not a collapse. Training is stable (no loss spikes > 0.5 after warmup).
notes: Run E2-20261122-132340-s0. Prediction check: r=4 within 3% of E0 (+2.0%) HIT; r=1 > +10% MISSED (+8.2%); r=2 < r=1 HIT; r=4 ~ r=6 HIT (+0.9%); r=8 <= r=4 MISSED (+2.3%); r=12 no collapse HIT but worse than 'slightly' (+5.7%); stability HIT (no spikes, max grad-norm 0.67). The loss is best at r=4 (= mean training r) and degrades when extrapolating: the loops don't converge to a fixed point. At 2.1x E1's FLOPs it is 5.8% worse than E1: no win per token or per FLOP at this scale.

title: Ternary weights on the E1 stack
question: How much quality does BitNet b1.58 ternary weights (-1, 0, +1) cost at our tiny scale? E1's exact layout and recipe, with only the weights changed, so any gap is down to ternary alone. (Ternary + loops, i.e. whether rounding error piles up across passes, is tested in E4.)
prediction: Written 2026-11-22, before any run. Full-val loss 0.605-0.645, i.e. +3.5% to +10% worse than E1 (0.5846), most likely around +6% (~0.62): roughly E0/E2 territory, so ternary gives back about all of E1's gain over dense. Reason: BitNet b1.58's own Table 1 shows a perplexity gap of +4.4% (loss +1.7%) at 700M that closes only at 3B; we are ~60x smaller than 700M, so the gap should be bigger. Training stays stable (no loss spikes > 0.5 after warmup) but runs 10-25% slower per token than E1, because the quantization is simulated in floating point (no ternary kernels). Payoff: weights 28.5 MB -> ~9.1 MB (2-bit packed); the non-embedding body 22.2 MB -> 2.8 MB (7.8x).
metrics: loss per bit of weight memory
notes: Designed 2026-11-22 (v0.3.4). Not run: training paused by the human. 33 BitLinear modules, 11.06M of 11.09M non-embedding params ternary. Deliberate deviations from the BitNet 2B4T recipe (no SubLN, SwiGLU not ReLU^2, single-stage schedule) keep it a one-ingredient change vs E1; the BitNet recipe is a possible follow-up if the gap is large.

title: Unlooped control for E2
question: Same 5 blocks as E2 ([SWA] [GDN, GDN, SWA] [attn]) trained once, without weight sharing or loops. Is weight sharing plus ~4 passes better than one pass of the same blocks? This separates the effect of looping from depth and parameter count.
prediction: Written 2026-11-22 before the run. E9 (5 unshared blocks, 9.17M non-emb, 0.079 GFLOP/token) lands at val loss 0.590-0.610: a bit worse than E1 (one fewer block) and about equal to E0. That would mean it BEATS E2 at r=4 (0.619) with 41% of the FLOPs, so at this scale looping the same blocks 4x is worse than running them once, untied. If instead E9 > 0.619, looping is genuinely buying something and E2 just pays for it in compute.

E10 = transformers 5.24.0 LlamaForCausalLM at E0's shapes: 13,767,552 total / 10,621,824 non-embedding params and 96.76M train FLOPs/token, all identical to E0 (computed, check k7_e10_parity.py). title: Negative-eigenvalue Gated DeltaNet for language modelling
question: Does letting GDN's write strength go negative (beta in (0, 2), i.e. negative eigenvalues) cost or help language modelling? E1's exact layout and recipe with one change (gdn_neg_eigval). Motivated by SQ6 arm (e): 100% parity in one pass and length generalisation, vs 97.9%/61.2% for looping (ledger C43).
prediction: Written 2026-11-22, before any run. Runs at E1's tuned LR (from K7), 3 seeds, same as E1's replication. Prediction: no language-modelling cost: mean full-val loss within +-1.0% of E1's mean, most likely within +-0.5%; training stable (no loss spikes > 0.5 after warmup; max grad-norm <= 1.5x E1's). Basis: the negative-eigenvalue paper (Grazzi et al., reported, not verified here) finds LM perplexity roughly unchanged while state tracking improves; our SQ6 shows the state-tracking gain at our scale. Criteria: 'free for LM' if |mean(E11) - mean(E1)| <= max(1%, 2x pooled seed std); 'helps LM' if mean(E11) < mean(E1) by more than 2x pooled std; 'hurts LM' if worse by more than 2x pooled std. If it is free or helps, the next step is neg-eig GDN inside the looped core (does it fix or replace what the loop was for?).
